Could you end up with more money invested than everything you earned working? Look at this scenario.
Imagine a fixed salary of three thousand dollars a month.
You set aside ten percent of that salary: three hundred dollars a month.
You invest it every month for forty years, from age twenty-five to sixty-five.
That's four hundred and eighty contributions.
Over forty years you earn one million four hundred and forty thousand dollars in total.
Out of your own pocket, you invest one hundred and forty-four thousand.
What would that be worth at the end?
Assume a fund that tracks the S&P 500,
and a constant ten percent compound annual return. An assumption, not a promise.
Year ten: about sixty thousand.
Year twenty: two hundred and fifteen thousand.
Year thirty: six hundred and nineteen thousand.
Year forty: one point six seven million.
Over sixty percent of that arrives in the last ten years.
Same scale, same forty years.
Total salary: one point four four million.
Final balance at ten percent: one point six seven million.
Only one hundred and forty-four thousand of that came out of your pocket.
In the simulation, the balance only overtakes total salary in year thirty-eight.
But real markets have down years.
Same example at seven percent a year:
the balance would be about seven hundred and forty-one thousand dollars.
Still about five times what you put in.
What this model assumes: a fixed salary, a constant return with dividends reinvested, and nominal dollars, with no fees, taxes or inflation.
With monthly contributions, the order of good and bad years also changes the result.
